title: Beyond the Harness: A Journey Towards Adaptative Engineering - Rajiv Chandegra, Annicha Labs
talk_summary: Rajiv argues fixed harnesses/factory-style agent orchestration are reliable for complicated problems but brittle for dynamic real-world 'messy' problems; he proposes adaptive engineering where engineers design constraints and the harness/roles emerge from local agent interactions. The talk is mostly conceptual, with few measured results or concrete implementation details.

takeaways.what_they_do: They propose starting with isomorphic agents and letting repeated local interactions plus feedback amplify small differences into specialized roles/niches.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the agent's identity isn't something you gave it. It's actually the position, role, or capability it took relative to the others

takeaways.what_they_do: They treat the rate/frequency of agent-to-agent interaction as a tunable lever rather than fixing handoff sequences up front.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your new lever uh becomes uh how the rate of coupling. Like, do you dial it up or do you dampen it down?

takeaways.what_they_do: They warn that emergent structures can settle into stable but suboptimal attractors, so you need genuine selection pressure or the system drifts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you need some sort of genuine selection pressure

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of hard-editing the workflow mid-run, the engineer monitors the emergent structure and adjusts constraints such as enablement, guardrails, rewards/costs, and speed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you are sensing it and responding to that rather than um stopping the engineering process and starting from scratch

takeaways.what_they_do: They argue diversity among agents is fuel for adaptation and warn that monoculture limits genuine diversity.
takeaways.evidence_quote: There is a risk of monoculture, where you don't get genuine diversity amongst agents because they're all trained on the same data.
